stimulus.text: Paraphrase: From April to June 1945, delegates from 50 nations met in San Francisco to write the charter of a new world organization. On June 26, 1945, they signed the United Nations Charter, which set out the purposes of the United Nations: to keep the peace, to settle disputes without war, and to encourage cooperation among nations. The Charter came into force on October 24, 1945, once enough nations, including the United States, had ratified it. The United States Senate approved the Charter by a wide margin, and the United States became a founding member.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary summary of the San Francisco Conference and the United Nations Charter, April to June 1945. Dates verified against the United Nations Charter record: signed June 26, 1945; in force October 24, 1945.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: What did the San Francisco Conference show about the changing role of the United States?

options.text: The United States had returned to isolation from world affairs
options.misconception: Joining the United Nations was the opposite of isolation; the United States took a leading role.

options.text: The United States had left the Allies to build the peace alone
options.misconception: The United States hosted the conference and shaped the Charter.

options.text: The United States had become the architect of the postwar order
The United States had given up its seat on the Security Council
options.misconception: The United States held a permanent Security Council seat from the start.

rationales.A: Background from the books: joining the United Nations was the opposite of isolation; the United States took a leading role.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the United States hosted the conference and shaped the Charter.
rationales.C: The United States hosted the conference and took a permanent Security Council seat, moving from wartime partner to builder of the postwar system.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the United States held a permanent Security Council seat from the start.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus says 50 nations met in San Francisco to write the Charter.
2. The United States hosted the meeting and became a founding member.
3. Background: after World War I, the United States had refused to join the League of Nations.
4. In 1945 it did the opposite, taking a permanent seat and helping to design the new organization.
Remember: hosting the conference that writes the rules is a sign of leadership, not of standing aside.
